name: Probability & Statistics
author: Recurse
subject: math
description: Averages, spread, probability rules, Bayes and expected value, and the traps that make data mislead.

lesson.intro: Statistics summarizes data, and probability reasons about uncertainty. Together they help you judge claims, risks and bets, and notice when a number is misleading you.

sections.title: Center and spread
sections.body:
Three numbers describe the center of a data set:

- Mean: add the values and divide by how many there are
- Median: the middle value after sorting (with an even count, average the two middle values)
- Mode: the most frequent value

The mean is pulled toward outliers. Salaries of 30k, 32k, 35k, 38k and 300k have a mean of 87k, yet four of the five people earn far less than that. The median, 35k, is a better picture of a typical person, which is why incomes and house prices are usually reported as medians. The mode is the only option for categories (the most common shoe size), but it can mislead when no value stands out or when the data has two separate peaks.

Center alone hides a lot. Two classes can both average 70 on a test while one has every score between 68 and 72 and the other ranges from 40 to 100. Measures of spread capture that difference:

- Range: maximum minus minimum. Easy, but it depends on only two values
- Variance: the average of the squared distances from the mean
- Standard deviation: the square root of the variance, back in the data's own units

Dividing by n gives the population variance. When the data is a sample from a bigger population, statisticians divide by n − 1 instead, which makes the estimate slightly larger.
sections.code:
Data: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9
Mean = 40 / 8 = 5
Distances from 5: −3, −1, −1, −1, 0, 0, 2, 4
Squared: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16   (sum 32)
Variance = 32 / 8 = 4
Standard deviation = √4 = 2

check.question: Five houses on a street sold for 200k, 210k, 220k, 230k and 2,000k. Which number best describes a typical price?
choices: The mean, 572k
The median, 220k
The average of the extremes, 1,100k
The range, 1,800k
check.explanation: One 2,000k sale drags the mean up to 572k, more than double what four of the five houses sold for. The median, 220k, does not care how extreme the outlier is. The range measures spread, not a typical value.

sections.title: Probability rules
sections.body:
When outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. Rolling an even number on a die: 3 favorable out of 6, so 1/2. Every probability is between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

The complement of an event is everything else: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). It is the fastest route to "at least one" questions. The chance of at least one six in four rolls is 1 minus the chance of no sixes: 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 1 − 0.482 = 0.518.

Two events are independent when one happening does not change the probability of the other, like two separate coin flips. For independent events, multiply:

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

For "or", add and then subtract the overlap you counted twice:

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

Independence also means no memory. After five heads in a row, a fair coin is still 1/2 heads on the next flip. Believing tails is "due" is called the gambler's fallacy.

check.question: You flip a fair coin 3 times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
check.explanation: The only way to get no heads is TTT, with probability (1/2)³ = 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. 1/8 is the chance of no heads, the complement you were meant to subtract, and 3/8 is the chance of exactly one head.

sections.title: Conditional probability and base rates
sections.body:
P(A | B) means the probability of A given that B has happened. Knowing B shrinks the world you are counting in:

P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

From a standard deck, P(king) = 4/52, but P(king | face card) = 4/12 = 1/3, because only the 12 face cards are still in play.

The order matters. P(tall | basketball player) is high, but P(basketball player | tall) is tiny, because there are far more tall people than basketball players. Bayes' rule connects the two directions:

P(A | B) = P(B | A) × P(A) / P(B)

The P(A) term is the base rate: how common A is before you see any evidence. Ignoring it is one of the most common probability mistakes. The easiest fix is to count imaginary people instead of juggling formulas.

Suppose 1% of people have a disease. A test is positive for 90% of sick people, and also for 9% of healthy people. Picture 1,000 people:
sections.code:
1,000 people, 1% sick
Sick:      10  →   9 test positive   (90%)
Healthy:  990  →  89 test positive   (9%)
P(sick | positive) = 9 / (9 + 89) ≈ 0.09
sections.tip: Most positives come from the huge healthy group, so a positive result here means about a 9% chance of disease, not 90%.

check.question: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. You draw one, do not put it back, and draw again. Given the first marble was red, what is the probability the second is red?
check.explanation: After one red is removed, 4 marbles remain and 2 of them are red, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2. 3/5 ignores the first draw; 3/10 is the probability that both draws are red, which is a different question.

sections.title: Expected value
sections.body:
Expected value is the long-run average result of a random process. Multiply each outcome by its probability and add the results:

E = (value₁ × p₁) + (value₂ × p₂) + ...

For a fair die, E = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 3.5. You can never roll a 3.5; expected value is an average over many trials, not a prediction for one.

Expected value is how to judge a bet. Count each outcome as a gain or loss relative to what you paid. If a game costs 2 dollars and pays 10 dollars when you roll a six, you net 8 dollars with probability 1/6 and lose 2 dollars with probability 5/6. Over many games you lose about 33 cents each time, however exciting the wins feel.

Expected values add: the expected total of two dice is 3.5 + 3.5 = 7. This holds even when the quantities are not independent, which makes it a powerful shortcut.

check.question: A raffle sells 100 tickets at 5 dollars each, and one ticket wins 200 dollars. What is the expected net value of buying one ticket?
choices: 2 dollars
−5 dollars
−3 dollars
195 dollars
check.explanation: Expected winnings are 200 × 1/100 = 2 dollars. Subtract the 5 dollar price: 2 − 5 = −3 dollars. 2 dollars forgets the ticket price, and 195 dollars is the net result only if you win.

sections.title: Correlation, causation and sampling
sections.body:
Correlation measures how closely two variables move together. The correlation coefficient r runs from −1 (a perfect downward line) through 0 (no straight-line pattern) to +1 (a perfect upward line). An r near 0 rules out a linear relationship, not every relationship; a U-shaped pattern can have r = 0.

Correlation does not show causation. When X and Y move together, there are several possible explanations:

- X causes Y
- Y causes X (reverse causation)
- A third factor, a confounder, drives both
- Coincidence, especially when many variables were searched for patterns

Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, but hot weather causes both. The reliable way to show causation is a randomized experiment: assign the treatment by chance, so that confounders end up balanced between the groups.

Sampling bias happens when the way data is collected makes some people more likely to be counted than others. Online polls count only people who choose to answer. Studying only successful companies ignores the ones that failed with the same habits (survivorship bias). A bigger sample does not fix bias; a million self-selected answers are still self-selected. Random sampling, where everyone has a known chance of being chosen, does.

check.question: A study finds that children in homes with more books score higher on reading tests. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Buying more books will raise a child's reading score
High reading scores cause parents to buy more books
Books and scores are associated, but something like parental education could drive both
The pattern must be a coincidence
check.explanation: An observational study shows association only. Parents' education or income could lead to both more books and higher scores. Concluding that buying books raises scores skips over that confounder; testing it would take an experiment.

keyTerms.definition: The middle value of sorted data; unlike the mean, it is barely moved by outliers.
The square root of the variance; a typical distance of values from the mean, in the data's own units.
The event that A does not happen; P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
P(A | B), the probability of A given that B has happened, equal to P(A and B) / P(B).
How common something is in the population before any specific evidence is considered.
The long-run average outcome: the sum of each value times its probability.
A third variable that influences two others, creating a correlation between them without direct causation.

summary: The mean is pulled by outliers, so the median is safer for skewed data; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
For "at least one" problems, compute 1 minus the chance of none; multiply probabilities only for independent events.
P(A | B) is not P(B | A): when a condition is rare, most positive tests can still be false positives.
Expected value is the long-run average: multiply each outcome by its probability and add.
Correlation does not prove causation, and a large biased sample is still biased.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why a positive result on a 90% accurate test for a rare disease probably does not mean they have it, using 1,000 imaginary people.

questions.question: What is the median of 7, 3, 9, 1, 12, 5?
questions.explanation: Sort first: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12. With six values, average the two middle ones: (5 + 7)/2 = 6. Taking the middle of the unsorted list (9 and 1) is the usual mistake.

questions.question: A company pays most staff between 40k and 60k, and its CEO earns 2 million. How do the mean and median salary compare?
choices: The mean is far above the median
The median is far above the mean
They are about equal, since most salaries are similar
The median is pulled up to match the mean
questions.explanation: One huge value drags the mean upward, while the median only depends on the middle position and stays near 50k. That is why the median better describes a typical employee here.

questions.question: The data 1, 3, 5, 7 has mean 4. What is its variance (dividing by n)?
questions.explanation: Distances from 4: −3, −1, 1, 3. Squares: 9, 1, 1, 9, which sum to 20. Divide by n = 4: variance = 5. The standard deviation is √5 ≈ 2.24.

questions.question: Data set A is 10, 10, 10, 10. Data set B is 0, 5, 15, 20. Which statement is true?
choices: Same mean and the same standard deviation
B has the larger mean
A has the larger standard deviation
Same mean, but B has a larger standard deviation
questions.explanation: Both means are 40/4 = 10. Every value in A equals the mean, so its standard deviation is 0, while B's values sit 5 to 10 away from the mean. The mean alone cannot tell the two sets apart.

questions.question: Why do we take the square root of the variance to get the standard deviation?
questions.answer: Variance is in squared units, such as dollars squared. Taking the square root returns the spread to the data's own units, so it can be compared directly with the values and the mean.
questions.explanation: Squaring the distances makes them all positive and weights big ones heavily, but leaves odd units. If heights are in cm, the variance is in cm², while the standard deviation is back in cm.

questions.question: A spinner has 8 equal sections, and 3 of them are red. What is the probability of NOT landing on red?
questions.explanation: P(red) = 3/8, so P(not red) = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 = 0.625. Counting directly works too: 5 of the 8 sections are not red.

questions.question: Each day has a 0.3 chance of rain, independent of other days. What is the probability it rains on both Saturday and Sunday?
questions.explanation: For independent events, multiply: 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09. Adding (0.6) answers a different question and would exceed 1 for larger probabilities.

questions.question: A fair coin has landed heads 6 times in a row. What is the probability the next flip is heads?
choices: Less than 1/2, because tails is due
More than 1/2, because heads is on a streak
questions.explanation: Flips are independent and the coin has no memory, so the next flip is still 1/2. 1/128 is the chance of seven heads in a row judged before any flips, which is not the question once six have already happened.

questions.question: A player makes each free throw with probability 0.7, independently. What is the probability she makes at least one of her next 2 shots?
questions.explanation: Use the complement. P(miss both) = 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09, so P(at least one) = 1 − 0.09 = 0.91. Adding 0.7 + 0.7 = 1.4 is impossible for a probability, a sign that the events overlap.

questions.question: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. What is P(A or B)?
questions.explanation: P(A or B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. Simply adding gives 0.9, which counts the outcomes where both happen twice.

questions.question: In a class of 30, 12 students play an instrument, and 9 of those 12 also sing. If a student plays an instrument, what is the probability they sing?
questions.explanation: Given that the student plays an instrument, only those 12 students count: P(sing | instrument) = 9/12 = 0.75. Dividing by all 30 students gives 0.3, which is P(plays and sings), not the conditional probability.

questions.question: A disease affects 2% of people. A test is positive for 95% of sick people and for 5% of healthy people. Roughly what share of people who test positive are actually sick?
choices: About 95%
About 50%
About 2%
About 28%
questions.explanation: Picture 10,000 people. 200 are sick and 190 of them test positive. 9,800 are healthy and 5% of them, 490, also test positive. P(sick | positive) = 190 / (190 + 490) ≈ 0.28. 95% is P(positive | sick), the reverse conditional.

questions.question: What is a base rate, and why does ignoring it mislead people?
questions.answer: The base rate is how common something is before you see any evidence, such as the share of people who have a disease. When it is rare, even an accurate test produces more false positives than true positives, so ignoring the base rate makes evidence look far more convincing than it is.
questions.explanation: In Bayes' rule the base rate P(A) multiplies everything. A small base rate pulls P(A | evidence) down, which is why screening results for rare conditions are confirmed with a second test.

questions.question: A game pays 12 dollars if you roll a 6 on a fair die and nothing otherwise. What is the expected payout per roll, in dollars?
questions.explanation: E = 12 × 1/6 + 0 × 5/6 = 2. If the game cost more than 2 dollars to play, you would lose money over time.

questions.question: A bet costs 1 dollar. With probability 0.3 you receive 3 dollars back (your total payout); otherwise you get nothing. What is the expected net gain per bet?
choices: −0.10 dollars
0.90 dollars
0.20 dollars
−0.70 dollars
questions.explanation: Expected payout: 0.3 × 3 = 0.90 dollars. Subtract the 1 dollar cost: −0.10 dollars per bet. 0.20 treats the 3 dollars as pure profit, but 1 dollar of it is your own stake coming back.

questions.question: Cities with more firefighters tend to have more fire damage each year. What best explains this correlation?
choices: Firefighters cause more fire damage
A strong correlation proves one causes the other
Larger cities have both more fires and more firefighters
The data must be wrong, since the two are unrelated
questions.explanation: City size is a confounder: bigger cities have more buildings that can burn and hire more firefighters. Concluding that firefighters cause damage confuses correlation with causation.

questions.question: A website asks visitors whether they like the site, and 90% vote yes. Why is this weak evidence that most people like it?
choices: It would be strong evidence if more people voted
90% is within the margin of error of 50%
Only visitors who chose to vote are counted, so the sample is biased
Opinions cannot be measured with percentages
questions.explanation: The voters selected themselves, and people who visit a site and bother to vote are likely fans. Collecting more votes the same way repeats the same bias; only a random sample of the wider population fixes it.
